claim: Head movements are primarily sensed in a reference frame tied to the head.
source: Head movements are primarily sensed in a reference frame tied to the head, yet they are used to calculate self-orientation relative to the world.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about how vestibular organs function.

claim: Head movements are used to calculate self-orientation relative to the world.
source: Head movements are primarily sensed in a reference frame tied to the head, yet they are used to calculate self-orientation relative to the world.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about spatial orientation.

claim: Calculating self-orientation relative to the world requires re-encoding head kinematic signals into a reference frame anchored to earth-centered landmarks such as gravity.
source: This requires to re-encode head kinematic signals into a reference frame anchored to earth-centered landmarks such as gravity, through computations whose neuronal substrate remains to be determined.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the need to transform head-bound signals into earth-bound orientation.

claim: The neuronal substrate for re-encoding head kinematic signals into an earth-centered reference frame remains to be determined.
source: This requires to re-encode head kinematic signals into a reference frame anchored to earth-centered landmarks such as gravity, through computations whose neuronal substrate remains to be determined.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: The rat caudal cerebellar vermis is essential for graviceptive functions.
source: Here, we studied the encoding of self-generated head movements in the rat caudal cerebellar vermis, an area essential for graviceptive functions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to lesion studies mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: Most Purkinje cells in the caudal cerebellar vermis exhibited a mixed sensitivity to head rotational and gravitational information.
source: We found that, contrarily to peripheral vestibular inputs, most Purkinje cells exhibited a mixed sensitivity to head rotational and gravitational information and were differentially modulated by active and passive movements.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: Purkinje cells in the caudal cerebellar vermis were differentially modulated by active and passive movements.
source: We found that, contrarily to peripheral vestibular inputs, most Purkinje cells exhibited a mixed sensitivity to head rotational and gravitational information and were differentially modulated by active and passive movements.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: A subpopulation of Purkinje cells in the caudal cerebellar vermis is tuned to rotations about an axis defined relative to gravity.
source: In a subpopulation of cells, this mixed sensitivity underlay a tuning to rotations about an axis defined relative to gravity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The caudal vermis hosts a re-encoded, gravitationally polarized representation of self-generated head kinematics in freely moving rats.
source: Therefore, we show that the caudal vermis hosts a re-encoded, gravitationally polarized representation of self-generated head kinematics in freely moving rats.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: Self-orientation is largely dependent on modalities that document head movements, including neck proprioception, optic flow and vestibular inputs.
source: Self-orientation is largely dependent on modalities that document head movements, including neck proprioception, optic flow and, most notably, vestibular inputs (Angelaki and Cullen, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Angelaki and Cullen, 2008.

claim: Vestibular signals are essential for stabilizing gaze.
source: Vestibular signals are essential for stabilizing gaze (du Lac et al., 1995) and for computing head direction, spatial maps and navigation trajectories (Stackman et al., 2005; Yoder and Taube, 2014; Wallace et al., 2002; Klier and Angelaki, 2008; Rochefort et al., 2011; Rochefort et al., 2013; Rondi-Reig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to du Lac et al., 1995.

claim: Vestibular signals are essential for computing head direction, spatial maps and navigation trajectories.
source: Vestibular signals are essential for stabilizing gaze (du Lac et al., 1995) and for computing head direction, spatial maps and navigation trajectories (Stackman et al., 2005; Yoder and Taube, 2014; Wallace et al., 2002; Klier and Angelaki, 2008; Rochefort et al., 2011; Rochefort et al., 2013; Rondi-Reig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Vestibular signals originate from two categories of skull-anchored inertial sensors: gyroscope-like structures (semi-circular canals) and accelerometer-like structures (otolith organs).
source: These signals originate from two categories of skull-anchored inertial sensors: gyroscope-like structures (semi-circular canals), which transduce head angular velocity, and accelerometer-like structures (otolith organs), which are activated indifferently by accelerated linear motion and by gravity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vestibular anatomy and function.

claim: Semi-circular canals transduce head angular velocity.
source: These signals originate from two categories of skull-anchored inertial sensors: gyroscope-like structures (semi-circular canals), which transduce head angular velocity, and accelerometer-like structures (otolith organs), which are activated indifferently by accelerated linear motion and by gravity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vestibular physiology.

claim: Otolith organs are activated indifferently by accelerated linear motion and by gravity.
source: These signals originate from two categories of skull-anchored inertial sensors: gyroscope-like structures (semi-circular canals), which transduce head angular velocity, and accelerometer-like structures (otolith organs), which are activated indifferently by accelerated linear motion and by gravity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about otolith organ function.

claim: Gravity provides an absolute directional cue on the external world.
source: Gravity provides an absolute directional cue on the external world and is effectively derived from vestibular inputs in the vestibular system (Merfeld et al., 1999; Angelaki et al., 1999), allowing the brain to align the axes of eye rotations with the direction of gravity (Hess and Angelaki, 1997; Hess and Angelaki, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about gravity as a reference.

claim: Gravity is effectively derived from vestibular inputs in the vestibular system.
source: Gravity provides an absolute directional cue on the external world and is effectively derived from vestibular inputs in the vestibular system (Merfeld et al., 1999; Angelaki et al., 1999), allowing the brain to align the axes of eye rotations with the direction of gravity (Hess and Angelaki, 1997; Hess and Angelaki, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Merfeld et al., 1999 and Angelaki et al., 1999.

claim: The brain aligns the axes of eye rotations with the direction of gravity.
source: Gravity provides an absolute directional cue on the external world and is effectively derived from vestibular inputs in the vestibular system (Merfeld et al., 1999; Angelaki et al., 1999), allowing the brain to align the axes of eye rotations with the direction of gravity (Hess and Angelaki, 1997; Hess and Angelaki, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hess and Angelaki, 1997 and 2003.

claim: Head direction cells are anchored to a reference frame aligned with gravity rather than to the animal's locomotor plane.
source: Head direction cells are also anchored to a reference frame aligned with gravity rather than to the animal's locomotor plane (Taube et al., 2013; Finkelstein et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2016; Olson et al., 2017); their activity, which relies on the temporal integration of head angular velocity signals (Song and Wang, 2005), thus also requires information on head orientation relative to gravity (head tilt) (Yoder and Taube, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Head direction cell activity relies on the temporal integration of head angular velocity signals.
source: Head direction cells are also anchored to a reference frame aligned with gravity rather than to the animal's locomotor plane (Taube et al., 2013; Finkelstein et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2016; Olson et al., 2017); their activity, which relies on the temporal integration of head angular velocity signals (Song and Wang, 2005), thus also requires information on head orientation relative to gravity (head tilt) (Yoder and Taube, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Song and Wang, 2005.

claim: Head direction cell activity requires information on head orientation relative to gravity (head tilt).
source: Head direction cells are also anchored to a reference frame aligned with gravity rather than to the animal's locomotor plane (Taube et al., 2013; Finkelstein et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2016; Olson et al., 2017); their activity, which relies on the temporal integration of head angular velocity signals (Song and Wang, 2005), thus also requires information on head orientation relative to gravity (head tilt) (Yoder and Taube, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoder and Taube, 2009.

claim: Identical activations of semi-circular canals may affect the azimuth and elevation of the head in very different ways depending on head tilt.
source: Indeed, identical activations of semi-circular canals may affect the azimuth and elevation of the head in very different ways depending on head tilt: for example, a rotation about the interaural axis will lead opposite changes of azimuth if the head is tilted with the left or right ear down.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the geometry of head rotations relative to gravity.

claim: A rotation about the interaural axis will lead to opposite changes of azimuth if the head is tilted with the left or right ear down.
source: Indeed, identical activations of semi-circular canals may affect the azimuth and elevation of the head in very different ways depending on head tilt: for example, a rotation about the interaural axis will lead opposite changes of azimuth if the head is tilted with the left or right ear down.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the geometry of head rotations.

claim: Lesion data suggest that the caudal cerebellar vermis plays a pivotal role in the discrimination of gravity.
source: Lesion data suggest that the caudal cerebellar vermis, a brain region receiving multimodal sensory cues related to head kinematics and orientation (Quy et al., 2011; Yakusheva et al., 2013), plays a pivotal role in the discrimination of gravity (e.g. Kim et al., 2015; Tarnutzer et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2015; Tarnutzer et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017.

claim: The caudal cerebellar vermis receives multimodal sensory cues related to head kinematics and orientation.
source: Lesion data suggest that the caudal cerebellar vermis, a brain region receiving multimodal sensory cues related to head kinematics and orientation (Quy et al., 2011; Yakusheva et al., 2013), plays a pivotal role in the discrimination of gravity (e.g. Kim et al., 2015; Tarnutzer et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Quy et al., 2011 and Yakusheva et al., 2013.

claim: A distinct population of caudal cerebellar Purkinje cells in monkeys dynamically reports head tilt during passive whole-body movements.
source: Moreover, a distinct population of caudal cerebellar Purkinje cells in monkeys dynamically reports head tilt during passive whole-body movements (Yakusheva et al., 2007; Laurens et al., 2013a; Laurens et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yakusheva et al., 2007; Laurens et al., 2013a; Laurens et al., 2013b.

claim: Passive movements only covered the lower range of frequencies and amplitudes observed during active self-motion.
source: However, these movements only covered the lower range of frequencies and amplitudes observed during active self-motion (Carriot et al., 2014; Carriot et al., 2015; Pasquet et al., 2016; Carriot et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carriot et al., 2014, 2015, 2017 and Pasquet et al., 2016.

claim: Early vestibular information processing is remarkably linear.
source: Moreover, despite the remarkable linearity of early vestibular information processing (Bagnall et al., 2008; but see Massot et al., 2011 and Sadeghi et al., 2007), the high amplitude of active movements might recruit vestibular afferents in a non-linear way (Hullar et al., 2005; Schneider et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bagnall et al., 2008, with caveats from Massot et al., 2011 and Sadeghi et al., 2007.

claim: The high amplitude of active movements might recruit vestibular afferents in a non-linear way.
source: Moreover, despite the remarkable linearity of early vestibular information processing (Bagnall et al., 2008; but see Massot et al., 2011 and Sadeghi et al., 2007), the high amplitude of active movements might recruit vestibular afferents in a non-linear way (Hullar et al., 2005; Schneider et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hullar et al., 2005 and Schneider et al., 2015.

claim: Studies in mice and monkeys have revealed that active and passive head movements are processed in fundamentally different ways within the vestibular nuclei.
source: In addition, studies in mice and monkeys have revealed that active and passive head movements are processed in fundamentally different ways within the vestibular nuclei (McCrea et al., 1999; Cullen and Roy, 2004; Roy and Cullen, 2004), which are highly interconnected with the caudal cerebellar vermis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to McCrea et al., 1999; Cullen and Roy, 2004; Roy and Cullen, 2004.

claim: The vestibular nuclei are highly interconnected with the caudal cerebellar vermis.
source: In addition, studies in mice and monkeys have revealed that active and passive head movements are processed in fundamentally different ways within the vestibular nuclei (McCrea et al., 1999; Cullen and Roy, 2004; Roy and Cullen, 2004), which are highly interconnected with the caudal cerebellar vermis.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Combined recordings of cerebellar activity and head movements were obtained in 16 freely moving rats.
source: Combined recordings of cerebellar activity and head movements were obtained in 16 freely moving rats (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and sample size.

claim: Head rotations occurred more frequently and swiftly along the pitch and yaw axes than along the roll axis.
source: In average, head rotations occurred more frequently and swiftly along the pitch and yaw axes than along the roll axis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), with typical angular speed in the 18–287 °/s range (average 2.5–97.5% percentiles calculated for velocities >15 °/s, n = 16 rats).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Typical angular speed during spontaneous head movements was in the 18–287 °/s range.
source: In average, head rotations occurred more frequently and swiftly along the pitch and yaw axes than along the roll axis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), with typical angular speed in the 18–287 °/s range (average 2.5–97.5% percentiles calculated for velocities >15 °/s, n = 16 rats).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Angular velocity signals displayed multi-peaked power spectra spanning frequencies up to 20 Hz.
source: Angular velocity (Ω) signals displayed multi-peaked power spectra spanning frequencies up to 20 Hz (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and showed strong temporal autocorrelation over a short timescale (<0.2 s, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Angular velocity signals showed strong temporal autocorrelation over a short timescale (<0.2 s).
source: Angular velocity (Ω) signals displayed multi-peaked power spectra spanning frequencies up to 20 Hz (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and showed strong temporal autocorrelation over a short timescale (<0.2 s, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Gravitational acceleration accounted for almost all (99%) of the power of the acceleration below 2 Hz.
source: AG accounted for almost all (99%) of the power of the acceleration below 2 Hz, and for only 9% of it in the 2–20 Hz range (n = 16 rats, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), indicating that the low-frequency component of acceleration (<2 Hz) mostly contained head tilt information.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Gravitational acceleration accounted for only 9% of the power of acceleration in the 2–20 Hz range.
source: AG accounted for almost all (99%) of the power of the acceleration below 2 Hz, and for only 9% of it in the 2–20 Hz range (n = 16 rats, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), indicating that the low-frequency component of acceleration (<2 Hz) mostly contained head tilt information.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The low-frequency component of acceleration (<2 Hz) mostly contained head tilt information.
source: AG accounted for almost all (99%) of the power of the acceleration below 2 Hz, and for only 9% of it in the 2–20 Hz range (n = 16 rats, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), indicating that the low-frequency component of acceleration (<2 Hz) mostly contained head tilt information.
evidence: This is an inference from the data showing that gravitational acceleration dominates low frequencies.

claim: Gravitational acceleration displayed temporal autocorrelation over long timescales (<5 s).
source: Consistent with this, AG displayed temporal autocorrelation over long timescales (<5 s, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Non-gravitational acceleration signals arose primarily from head rotations.
source: AnG varied at the same timescale as Ω and exhibited the same order of magnitude, and temporal correlation pattern with Ω , as linear tangential acceleration predicted from head rotations (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E and Appendix). This suggests that, in our conditions, AnG signals arose primarily from head rotations.
evidence: This is an inference supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: A total of 86 units were recorded.
source: A total of 86 units were recorded (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C) and classified into putative Purkinje cells (90%), Golgi cells (5%) and mossy fibers (5%) using established criteria (Van Dijck et al., 2013, see Figure 1—figure supplement 3E and Appendix).
evidence: This describes the sample size of recorded units.

claim: Recorded units were classified into putative Purkinje cells (90%), Golgi cells (5%) and mossy fibers (5%).
source: A total of 86 units were recorded (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C) and classified into putative Purkinje cells (90%), Golgi cells (5%) and mossy fibers (5%) using established criteria (Van Dijck et al., 2013, see Figure 1—figure supplement 3E and Appendix).
evidence: This is based on classification using established criteria from Van Dijck et al., 2013.

claim: Putative Purkinje cells exhibited irregular inter-spike intervals at rest with an average CV of 0.95 ± 0.58.
source: Putative Purkinje cells exhibited irregular inter-spike intervals (ISI) at rest (average CV: 0.95 ± 0.58, calculated for periods of immobility isolated from 76 cells), resulting in sharp fluctuations of the instantaneous firing rate even during immobility (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Firing rate predictability was greater when considering angular velocity combined with either acceleration or gravitational acceleration (mean R² = 0.17 ± 0.13 in both cases, n = 86 units).
source: Overall, we found that firing rate predictability was greater when considering Ω combined with either A or AG (mean R2 = 0.17 ± 0.13 in both cases, n = 86 units; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model-free analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: R² values were always greater for gravitational acceleration-based than for non-gravitational acceleration-based estimates (p<8e-9).
source: R2 values were always greater for AG-based than for AnG-based estimates (p<8e-9 for both AG vs. AnG and Ω + AG vs. Ω + AnG, n = 86 units), showing that gravitational information dominated the effect of acceleration on firing rate.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of model performance.

claim: Gravitational information dominated the effect of acceleration on firing rate.
source: R2 values were always greater for AG-based than for AnG-based estimates (p<8e-9 for both AG vs. AnG and Ω + AG vs. Ω + AnG, n = 86 units), showing that gravitational information dominated the effect of acceleration on firing rate.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of R² values.

claim: Cerebellar units preferentially exhibited a mixed sensitivity to head rotations and head tilt.
source: This analysis suggests that cerebellar units preferentially exhibited a mixed sensitivity to head rotations and head tilt.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model-free analysis results.

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficients between independent firing rate estimates were mostly above 0.5 (mean R = 0.65 ± 0.23, n = 86).
source: The Pearson correlation coefficients (R) between independent estimates were mostly above 0.5 (mean R = 0.65 ± 0.23, n = 86, top panel of Figure 1F) while the null distribution computed using shuffled spike trains exhibited significantly smaller R values centered near zero (mean R = 0.14 ± 0.10, n = 86 units; p=2.2 × 10−16, bottom panel of Figure 1F) showing the ability of our method to consistently capture the link between head movements and firing rate modulations.
evidence: This is a quantitative result demonstrating the robustness of the method.

claim: The instantaneous firing rate of neighboring units displayed positive correlations (R = 0.14 ± 0.26, n = 35 pairs, p=0.0014).
source: The instantaneous firing rate of neighboring units (Figure 2A) indeed displayed positive correlations (R = 0.14 ± 0.26, n = 35 pairs, p=0.0014, one-sampled Wilcoxon test) that were lost if the spike train of one unit was time-reversed (R = 0.00 ± 0.03, p=0.49, one-sampled Wilcoxon test, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of neighboring units.

claim: Correlations between neighboring units were lost if the spike train of one unit was time-reversed (R = 0.00 ± 0.03, p=0.49).
source: The instantaneous firing rate of neighboring units (Figure 2A) indeed displayed positive correlations (R = 0.14 ± 0.26, n = 35 pairs, p=0.0014, one-sampled Wilcoxon test) that were lost if the spike train of one unit was time-reversed (R = 0.00 ± 0.03, p=0.49, one-sampled Wilcoxon test, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a control analysis demonstrating that correlations are not artifactual.

claim: Correlations were higher when comparing firing rate estimates (R = 0.31 ± 0.47, p=0.0013) than when comparing instantaneous firing rates.
source: Correlations were higher (p=0.0074, paired Wilcoxon test) when comparing firing rate estimates (R = 0.31 ± 0.47, p=0.0013, one-sampled Wilcoxon test, Figure 2C) than when comparing instantaneous firing rates (Figure 2D), showing that neighboring unit tended to share similar sensitivities to head movements.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison showing shared sensitivity in neighboring units.

claim: Neighboring units tended to share similar sensitivities to head movements.
source: Correlations were higher (p=0.0074, paired Wilcoxon test) when comparing firing rate estimates (R = 0.31 ± 0.47, p=0.0013, one-sampled Wilcoxon test, Figure 2C) than when comparing instantaneous firing rates (Figure 2D), showing that neighboring unit tended to share similar sensitivities to head movements.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation analysis.

claim: The presence or absence of light did not change the correlation between independent estimates (p=0.87, paired Wilcoxon test, n = 23).
source: Overall, the presence or absence of light did not change the correlation between independent estimates (p=0.87, paired Wilcoxon test, n = 23, Figure 2E,F), showing a limited influence of visual cues on the units' sensitivity to head movements.
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing light vs. dark conditions.

claim: Visual cues had limited influence on the units' sensitivity to head movements.
source: Overall, the presence or absence of light did not change the correlation between independent estimates (p=0.87, paired Wilcoxon test, n = 23, Figure 2E,F), showing a limited influence of visual cues on the units' sensitivity to head movements.
evidence: This is an inference from the light vs. dark comparison.

claim: Firing rate estimates from passive sessions significantly differed from estimates obtained using observations from the active session (p=0.0021, paired Wilcoxon test, n = 17).
source: The resulting estimates significantly differed from estimates obtained using observations from the passive session (p=0.0021, paired Wilcoxon test, n = 17, Figure 2G,H), suggesting that in many cases the units' coding schemes differed when movements were self-generated or passively experienced.
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing active vs. passive conditions.

claim: The units' coding schemes differed when movements were self-generated or passively experienced.
source: The resulting estimates significantly differed from estimates obtained using observations from the passive session (p=0.0021, paired Wilcoxon test, n = 17, Figure 2G,H), suggesting that in many cases the units' coding schemes differed when movements were self-generated or passively experienced.
evidence: This is an inference from the active vs. passive comparison.

claim: 6 Ω-selective and 12 AG-selective units were isolated by picking cases for which the firing rate predictability was at least eightfold greater for one parameter than the other.
source: We isolated 6 Ω-selective and 12 AG-selective units by picking cases for which the firing rate predictability was at least eightfold greater for one parameter than the other (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the criteria for classifying selective units.

claim: Ω-units exhibited a bidirectional modulation of the firing rate by specific combinations of rotations.
source: These plots showed a bidirectional modulation of the firing rate by specific combinations of rotations, since the firing rate was increased or decreased at a lag close to 0, that is, close to the occurrence of specific rotation values (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the inertio-temporal receptive fields shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ω-units were tuned to specific 3D rotations.
source: 3D plots representing the firing rate as a function of the three components of Ω (calculated for the lag showing the strongest modulation of firing rate) revealed clear firing rate gradients along specific directions of rotation, showing that these units were tuned to specific 3D rotations (Figure 3C and Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the 3D plots in Figure 3C and Video 2.

claim: The gain calculated at the optimal lag was greater for Ω-units (0.28 ± 0.15 °⁻¹, n = 6) than for AG-units (0.03 ± 0.02 °⁻¹, n = 7, p=0.0012) and mixed units (0.07 ± 0.05 °⁻¹, n = 53, p=0.00022).
source: The gain calculated at the optimal lag was greater for Ω-units (0.28 ± 0.15 °−1, n = 6) than for AG-units and other units with mixed sensitivity (0.03 ± 0.02 °−1, n = 7, p=0.0012 and 0.07 ± 0.05 °−1, n = 53, p=0.00022, respectively; calculated only for units with a significant ωopt vector; see Appendix).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of rotational sensitivity across unit types.

claim: The optimal lag of Ω-units was centered around zero (0.5 ± 21.8 ms, n = 6).
source: The optimal lag of Ω-units was centered around zero (0.5 ± 21.8 ms, n = 6) while the one of mixed units was greater (29.8 ± 142.4 ms, n = 53), although not significantly (p=0.072).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of temporal dynamics.

claim: Ω-units corresponded to putative mossy fibers (n = 2) and putative Purkinje cells (n = 4).
source: Ω-units corresponded to putative mossy fibers (n = 2) and putative Purkinje cells (n = 4), and exhibited preferred rotation axes clustered around the excitatory direction of semi-circular canals (Figure 3F).
evidence: This describes the cell type classification of Ω-units.

claim: Ω-units exhibited preferred rotation axes clustered around the excitatory direction of semi-circular canals.
source: Ω-units corresponded to putative mossy fibers (n = 2) and putative Purkinje cells (n = 4), and exhibited preferred rotation axes clustered around the excitatory direction of semi-circular canals (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: AG-units were strongly modulated by head tilt with simple receptive fields.
source: The resulting plots confirmed that AG-units were strongly modulated by head tilt with simple receptive fields (region of increased firing rate; Figure 3H), contrarily to Ω-units which were not modulated by head tilt (the CV of firing rate across head tilts was higher for AG-units than for Ω-units: 2.28 vs. 0.29, p=0.0047, Figure 3I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the tilt-dependent rate maps in Figure 3H.

claim: Ω-units were not modulated by head tilt.
source: The resulting plots confirmed that AG-units were strongly modulated by head tilt with simple receptive fields (region of increased firing rate; Figure 3H), contrarily to Ω-units which were not modulated by head tilt (the CV of firing rate across head tilts was higher for AG-units than for Ω-units: 2.28 vs. 0.29, p=0.0047, Figure 3I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the low CV of firing rate across head tilts for Ω-units.

claim: AG-units were classified as putative mossy fibers (n = 1), Golgi cells (n = 3) and Purkinje cells (n = 8).
source: AG-units were classified as putative mossy fibers (n = 1), Golgi cells (n = 3) and Purkinje cells (n = 8).
evidence: This describes the cell type classification of AG-units.

claim: A fraction (20%) of caudal cerebellar units displayed selective tuning to either head angular velocity or head tilt.
source: Overall, these data show that a fraction (20%) of caudal cerebellar units displayed selective tuning to either head angular velocity or head tilt; most of our putative granular layer units (6/8) belonged to these categories.
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the classification of units.

claim: Most putative granular layer units (6/8) belonged to the Ω-selective or AG-selective categories.
source: Overall, these data show that a fraction (20%) of caudal cerebellar units displayed selective tuning to either head angular velocity or head tilt; most of our putative granular layer units (6/8) belonged to these categories.
evidence: This is a summary statistic about granular layer units.

claim: The rotational sensitivity of units with mixed sensitivity was often highly tilt-dependent.
source: As shown above, most units displayed a mixed sensitivity to rotational and gravitational information and were not classified as Ω-units or AG-units. A direct examination of inertio-temporal receptive fields for different head orientations showed that the rotational sensitivity of these units was indeed often highly tilt-dependent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the examples in Figure 4A–F.

claim: The stability index was lower for non-Ω-units (σx = 0.36 ± 0.32 and σy = 0.41 ± 0.29, n = 60) than for Ω-units (σx = 0.73 ± 0.13 and σy = 0.88 ± 0.06, n = 6; p=0.0027 and p=0.00011, respectively).
source: This index was lower for non-Ω-units (σx = 0.36 ± 0.32 and σy = 0.41 ± 0.29, n = 60) than for Ω-units (σx = 0.73 ± 0.13 and σy = 0.88 ± 0.06, n = 6; p=0.0027 and p=0.00011, respectively, Figure 4G,H), confirming that the rotational tuning of the largest fraction of our cell population was head tilt-dependent.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison demonstrating tilt-dependent rotational tuning.

claim: The rotational tuning of the largest fraction of the cell population was head tilt-dependent.
source: This index was lower for non-Ω-units (σx = 0.36 ± 0.32 and σy = 0.41 ± 0.29, n = 60) than for Ω-units (σx = 0.73 ± 0.13 and σy = 0.88 ± 0.06, n = 6; p=0.0027 and p=0.00011, respectively, Figure 4G,H), confirming that the rotational tuning of the largest fraction of our cell population was head tilt-dependent.
evidence: This is an inference from the stability index analysis.

claim: Units exhibiting a stronger tuning toward an external or internal coding scheme were isolated by setting a cutoff (difference between external and internal collinearity > 0.5 or < −0.5 for angular distances ranging 80–100°).
source: Units exhibiting a stronger tuning toward an external or internal coding scheme were isolated by setting a cutoff (difference between external and internal collinearity > 0.5 or < −0.5 for angular distances ranging 80–100 °).
evidence: This describes the criteria for classifying external vs. internal coding units.

claim: All units exhibiting stronger external or internal tuning corresponded to putative Purkinje cells.
source: All these units corresponded to putative Purkinje cells.
evidence: This describes the cell type of units with external/internal tuning.

claim: The preferred rotation axes of external-coding cells did not appear to cluster around specific directions.
source: The preferred rotation axes of external-coding cells did not appear to cluster around specific directions (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The rotational sensitivity of units was maximal for positive lags relative to angular velocity, suggesting that it was driven by sensory cues rather than by motor commands.
source: The rotational sensitivity of caudal cerebellar units was maximal for positive lags relative to angular velocity, suggesting that it was driven by sensory cues rather than by motor commands.
evidence: This is an inference from the temporal lag analysis.

claim: There was no evidence for a crucial role of visual inputs on the units' sensitivity to head movements.
source: By comparing the firing rate predicted from sessions recorded in different conditions, we found no evidence for a crucial role of visual inputs, but instead found differences in the sensitivity to active vs. passive movements.
evidence: This is based on the comparison of light vs. dark conditions shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: 'Global' linear models always produced poorer predictions than the model-free approach.
source: As shown in Figure 6A (for the linear model based on Ω, Ω˙ and AG) and in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 (for all other models), 'global' linear models always produced poorer predictions than our model-free approach.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparisons in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The firing rate predictability calculated with the model-free approach was not significantly different from the coefficient of determination calculated from 'local' linear models (p=0.24, paired Wilcoxon test, n = 86 units).
source: In contrast, the firing rate predictability calculated with our model-free approach was not significantly different from the coefficient of determination calculated from 'local' linear models used to generate tilt-dependent rotational sensitivity maps (p=0.24, paired Wilcoxon test, n = 86 units, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A series of 'local' linear fits of the unit's rotational sensitivity provide a description of the firing rate as performant as the model-free approach.
source: This nonlinearity appears to be mainly due to a dependency to head tilt of the (linear) rotational sensitivity, since a series of 'local' linear fits of the unit's rotational sensitivity (head-tilt dependent ωopt) collectively provide a description of the firing rate as performant as the model-free approach (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison in Figure 6B.

claim: The caudal cerebellar vermis hosts gravitationally polarized representations of head rotations in freely moving rats.
source: Our findings reveal that the caudal cerebellar vermis hosts gravitationally polarized representations of head rotations in freely moving rats.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: Most putative Purkinje cells in the posterior cerebellum exhibit receptive fields encoding head rotations about 3D axes anchored to the direction of gravity.
source: We found that most putative Purkinje cell in the posterior cerebellum indeed exhibit receptive fields encoding head rotations about 3D axes anchored to the direction of gravity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding, supported by the data in Figures 4-5.

claim: This type of rotational sensitivity requires a complex re-encoding of head-centered sensory cues.
source: This type of rotational sensitivity requires a complex re-encoding of head-centered sensory cues and might subserve downstream computations such as the encoding of head direction in the earth-horizontal plane.
evidence: This is an inference about the computational requirements of the observed coding scheme.

claim: Gravitationally polarized rotational sensitivity might subserve downstream computations such as the encoding of head direction in the earth-horizontal plane.
source: This type of rotational sensitivity requires a complex re-encoding of head-centered sensory cues and might subserve downstream computations such as the encoding of head direction in the earth-horizontal plane.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of the observed coding scheme.

claim: Studies in the vestibular and cerebellar nuclei during self-generated movements have provided strong indications that passive vs. active movements elicit different firing modulations in the same neurons.
source: The vestibular system has been mostly approached so far in head-fixed animals submitted to passive, externally applied, movements; however, studies in the vestibular and cerebellar nuclei during self-generated movements have provided strong indications that passive vs. active movements elicit different firing modulations in the same neurons (Cullen et al., 2011; Medrea and Cullen, 2013; Cullen and Brooks, 2015; Brooks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cullen et al., 2011; Medrea and Cullen, 2013; Cullen and Brooks, 2015; Brooks et al., 2015.

claim: The instantaneous firing rate of many units exhibited strong fluctuations even during complete immobility.
source: We found that the instantaneous firing rate of many units exhibited strong fluctuations even during complete immobility.
evidence: This is an observation from the data, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The instantaneous firing rate was only loosely connected to the rapid component of head inertial signals.
source: As a result, the instantaneous firing rate was only loosely connected to the rapid component of head inertial signals, consistent with a coding of information at the level of Purkinje cell populations (Herzfeld et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the observed firing rate fluctuations, supported by citation to Herzfeld et al., 2015.

claim: Neighboring putative Purkinje cells exhibited positive correlations of their firing rate and of the component of firing rate explained by inertial parameters.
source: In support of this interpretation, we found that neighboring putative Purkinje cells exhibited positive correlations of their firing rate and of the component of firing rate explained by inertial parameters (isolated with our model-free approach), indicating a similarity of the inertial receptive fields in cells likely belonging to the same microzone.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 2.

claim: The majority of units in the sample exhibited tilt-dependent rotational tuning.
source: The majority of units in our sample exhibited tilt-dependent rotational tuning.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cells tuned to rotations about an earth-bound axis are expected to exhibit a tilt-dependent sensitivity to head-bound rotations.
source: Therefore, cells tuned to rotations about an earth-bound axis are expected to exhibit a tilt-dependent sensitivity to head-bound rotations.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the geometry of coordinate transformations.

claim: Sets of Purkinje cells encoding rotations relative to gravity could subtract the component of rotations that changes head orientation relative to gravity from semi-circular canal inputs in vestibular nuclear neurons.
source: However, as noted previously by Yakusheva et al. (2008), sets of Purkinje cells (which are inhibitory neurons) encoding rotations relative to gravity (such as displayed in Figure 5C) could subtract the component of rotations that changes head orientation relative to gravity from semi-circular canal inputs in vestibular nuclear neurons; this operation would isolate an earth-horizontal component of head angular velocity suitable for the computation of azimuthal heading in head direction cells (Finkelstein et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role, supported by citation to Yakusheva et al., 2008 and Finkelstein et al., 2016.

claim: Subtracting gravity-aligned rotations would isolate an earth-horizontal component of head angular velocity suitable for the computation of azimuthal heading in head direction cells.
source: However, as noted previously by Yakusheva et al. (2008), sets of Purkinje cells (which are inhibitory neurons) encoding rotations relative to gravity (such as displayed in Figure 5C) could subtract the component of rotations that changes head orientation relative to gravity from semi-circular canal inputs in vestibular nuclear neurons; this operation would isolate an earth-horizontal component of head angular velocity suitable for the computation of azimuthal heading in head direction cells (Finkelstein et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about computational mechanisms, supported by citation to Finkelstein et al., 2016.

claim: The granular layer of the caudal vermis contains a high amount of unipolar brush cells.
source: The granular layer of the caudal vermis contains a high amount of unipolar brush cells (excitatory interneurons intercalated between mossy fibers and granule cells; Mugnaini et al., 2011) which may smooth otolithic signals over hundreds of milliseconds (van Dorp and De Zeeuw, 2014; Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015; Zampini et al., 2016) and thus provide a proxy of gravitational signals to granule cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mugnaini et al., 2011.

claim: Unipolar brush cells may smooth otolithic signals over hundreds of milliseconds.
source: The granular layer of the caudal vermis contains a high amount of unipolar brush cells (excitatory interneurons intercalated between mossy fibers and granule cells; Mugnaini et al., 2011) which may smooth otolithic signals over hundreds of milliseconds (van Dorp and De Zeeuw, 2014; Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015; Zampini et al., 2016) and thus provide a proxy of gravitational signals to granule cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to van Dorp and De Zeeuw, 2014; Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015; Zampini et al., 2016.

claim: Granule cells receiving convergent inputs carrying gravitational and rotational information could operate as coincidence detectors.
source: Granule cells receiving convergent inputs (Huang et al., 2013) carrying gravitational and rotational information could then operate as coincidence detectors (Chadderton et al., 2004; Chabrol et al., 2015) and signal the occurrence of specific combinations of rotation and head tilt to Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is speculation about circuit mechanisms, supported by citations to Huang et al., 2013; Chadderton et al., 2004; Chabrol et al., 2015.

claim: Purkinje cell receptive fields are shaped by the activity of climbing fibers which determine the sensitivity to subsets of granule cells (parallel fiber) afferents.
source: Purkinje cell receptive fields are shaped by the activity of climbing fibers which determine the sensitivity to subsets of granule cells (parallel fiber) afferents (e.g. Dean et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar learning, supported by citation to Dean et al., 2010.

claim: Vestibular climbing fibers emanate from inferior olive neurons of the β-nucleus.
source: Vestibular climbing fibers emanate from inferior olive neurons of the β-nucleus, which are controlled by dorsal Y-group and parasolitary nucleus afferents.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The dorsal Y-group and parasolitary nucleus carry rotational and low-pass filtered otolithic signals.
source: These nuclei carry rotational and low-pass filtered otolithic signals but are also under the influence of vestibulo-cerebellar Purkinje cells (Barmack and Yakhnitsa, 2000; Barmack, 2003; Wylie et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barmack and Yakhnitsa, 2000; Barmack, 2003; Wylie et al., 1994.

claim: The teaching signal sent to Purkinje cells by way of olivary neurons results from a complex interplay between external afferents and the action of Purkinje cells themselves.
source: Therefore, the teaching signal sent to Purkinje cells by way of olivary neurons shall result from a complex interplay between external afferents and the action of Purkinje cells themselves, leading to the observed tilt-dependent rotational sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference about circuit mechanisms.

claim: The dominant coding scheme of natural head kinematics in the caudal cerebellum is a tilt-dependent representation of head rotations.
source: In conclusion, our work reveals that the dominant coding scheme of natural head kinematics in the caudal cerebellum is a tilt-dependent representation of head rotations.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: The transformation of head-bound peripheral vestibular signals into an earth-bound representation of head kinematics involves complex nonlinear computations.
source: As emphasized previously (Green and Angelaki, 2007), the transformation of head-bound peripheral vestibular signals into an earth-bound representation of head kinematics involves complex nonlinear computations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Green and Angelaki, 2007.

claim: The detailed mechanisms underlying the computation of gravitationally polarized rotational receptive fields remain to be elucidated.
source: In particular, the detailed mechanisms underlying the computation of gravitationally polarized rotational receptive fields remain to be elucidated.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current understanding.

claim: The caudal cerebellar cortex is in a key anatomical position immediately downstream of the vestibular organs and upstream of the vestibular nuclei.
source: The presence of such receptive fields in the caudal cerebellar cortex, as shown here, as well as the key anatomical position of this structure immediately downstream of the vestibular organs and upstream of the vestibular nuclei, warrant a detailed examination of how the cerebellar cortical microcircuit might re-express head movements relative to gravity.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Sixteen adult male Long-Evans rats aged 3–4 months and weighing 250–300 g at surgery were used in this study.
source: Sixteen adult male Long-Evans rats (aged 3–4 months, 250–300 g at surgery, RRID:RGD_60991) were used in this study.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: Experimental procedures were conducted in conformity with institutional guidelines and in compliance with French national and European laws and policies.
source: Experimental procedures were conducted in conformity with the institutional guidelines and in compliance with French national and European laws and policies.
evidence: This describes ethical compliance.

claim: All procedures were approved by the 'Charles Darwin' Ethics Committee (project number 1334).
source: All procedures were approved by the 'Charles Darwin' Ethics Committee (project number 1334).
evidence: This describes ethical approval.
